subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Thomas, listen. I came back to Bengaluru at twenty after five years in Perth, and I expected to slide right in. Instead the city had moved without me: the lane had a new flyover, my friends had new jokes and I didn't know the auto fare. Worse, I had changed too. The noise was too much and my Kannada slow. I felt like a guest in my own house. My mother said, "Give it time. You're not late." I began small: I took the bus with a route written on my hand, went to the same bakery every Saturday, and asked my old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending. After some months I noticed I'd stopped feeling out of step. Nobody handed me a place. I built one slowly. Anjali

qa.q: How many years had Anjali spent in Perth?
qa.a: Anjali spent five years in Perth.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel back in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Anjali felt lost and out of step, like a guest in the family home, since both the city and Anjali had changed.

qa.q: What choices helped Anjali, and why?
qa.a: Asking an old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending, and building small routines like the bakery, so belonging grew slowly.

qa.q: What did Anjali's mother mean by You're not late?
qa.a: That there was no deadline for fitting in, and patience with the place and oneself was enough.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience brings a new fit.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Nikita landed in Pune after six years in Toronto, and her suitcase did not. The airline said tomorrow. Outside, monsoon rain hammered the taxi rank, drivers shouted prices in Marathi that Nikita understood but answered slowly, and the phone was almost dead. Cousin Kalyani finally found Nikita under the shed. "You look lost," Kalyani said, laughing gently. Nikita's eyes stung. The city had rebuilt itself, and the road to the old school now had a metro pillar in the middle. Even Nikita's own jokes sounded odd in this air. "I don't know who I am here," Nikita said in the car. Kalyani answered, "You're the one who ate all the mango pickle, remember? Give it a week. You'll get the auto rates back." Nikita smiled at the windshield.

qa.q: What did the airline say about the suitcase?
What was Nikita feeling in the car, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lost and out of step; Nikita's eyes stung and Nikita said not knowing who Nikita is here.

qa.q: What small step could help Nikita fit in again?
qa.a: Give it a week, relearn the auto rates and let familiar things like the mango pickle return.
As a familiar cousin beneath the changes who needs time; Kalyani laughed gently and recalled the mango pickle.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience begins a new fit.
